text:
# RFE Template

Scale the output to match the size of the RFE. Use the appropriate section set below.

## Evidence rule for `## Affected Customers` and `## Business Justification`

These two sections are what WHY is scored on. A reviewer scores WHY **1/2 instead of
2/2** whenever they contain no named account and no number — that single gap is the
most common deduction on RFEs produced from this template.

So both sections must carry, when the requester supplied them:

1. At least one **named** account, partner or segment — a proper noun, not a persona.
2. At least one **figure** — currency, percentage, count, or multiplier.
3. Attribution for each claim — who said it, or where it was measured.

Copy names and figures ACROSS from the requester's answers CHARACTER-FOR-CHARACTER.
Do not round, re-word, average, or replace a name with the category it belongs to.

### Worked example — the same input, written two ways

Requester's answers:

> Customers: Enterprise platform engineering teams at Crestview Investments,
> DataPulse, and Frontier Banking; SRE teams managing ML infrastructure.
> Business justification: Expected 10x increase in non-data-scientist users by
> removing the Python-only barrier. 90% reduction in pipeline complexity. Every
> major competitor provides CLI tooling — table stakes for enterprise adoption.

WRONG — scores WHY 1/2. Every name and number has been deleted; "enterprise
customers" and "significant" are the categories the evidence belonged to:

```markdown
## Affected Customers
Enterprise platform engineering teams and SRE personas managing ML infrastructure.

## Business Justification
Adoption is limited by the Python-only barrier. Adding a CLI would significantly
broaden the addressable user base and is important for enterprise competitiveness.
```

RIGHT — scores WHY 2/2. Same facts, carried across verbatim and attributed:

```markdown
## Affected Customers
- Crestview Investments, DataPulse, Frontier Banking — enterprise platform
  engineering teams (named by the requester as affected accounts).
- SRE teams managing ML infrastructure; DevOps engineers building CI/CD for ML.

## Business Justification
- **Reach:** requester expects a 10x increase in non-data-scientist users (SREs,
  platform engineers) once the Python-only barrier is removed.
- **Efficiency:** 90% reduction in pipeline complexity for cluster-management
  automation.
- **Competitive:** every major competitor ships CLI tooling; the requester
  describes this as table stakes for enterprise adoption.
```

### When the requester supplied no evidence

State the absence plainly and specifically. A visible gap is scored better than
invented evidence, and the reviewer needs to see it in order to flag it:

```markdown
## Affected Customers
None identified. Raised as an internal platform observation; no customer,
prospect, or field request is on record.

## Business Justification
No revenue impact, customer escalation, or competitive pressure was identified.
The stated driver is recurring maintenance overhead reported by the platform team.
```

Never invent a customer name, revenue figure, percentage, escalation, or
competitive claim that the requester did not give you.

## Framing rule for `## Summary`, `## Acceptance Criteria` and `title`

A reviewer scores "Not a task" **1/2 or 0/2** when the RFE reads as engineering work
to be done rather than a capability a user gains. Two mechanical habits prevent it:

1. **Every acceptance-criterion line starts with the user as its subject** — `User
   can …`, `Data scientists can …`, `Operators can …`. Never start one with a
   component, a pipeline stage, or a CI job as the subject.
2. **The title and Summary name the capability, not the activity.** Not "Rename X",
   "Align X with Y", "Add a CI check for X" — instead the user-visible outcome that
   the rename/alignment/check exists to deliver.

Worked example — an internal version-drift chore:

WRONG — scores Not-a-task 1/2. Title and criteria are the work items:

```markdown
title: Align KFP SDK version in workbench images with the pipelines server

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] KFP SDK version in workbench images matches the version shipped with the server
- [ ] CI check fails the image build if the workbench SDK version does not match
```

RIGHT — scores Not-a-task 2/2. Same underlying need, stated as user capability:

```markdown
title: Pipelines authored in a workbench run without SDK/server incompatibility

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Data scientists can compile and submit a pipeline from a stock workbench image
      and have it run without version-incompatibility errors
- [ ] Data scientists no longer need to check or pin SDK versions themselves before
      submitting a pipeline
```

Describing the outcome this way does NOT prescribe HOW — it leaves the team free to
deliver it by pinning, by CI enforcement, or by any other means.

## Open-to-HOW rule for `## Acceptance Criteria` and `### In Scope`

Naming a platform technology is allowed — but only in one of two roles. A reviewer
scores "Open to HOW" **1/2** the moment a technology becomes the thing being
mandated rather than an example or a boundary.

1. **A technology may name the domain** (title, `## Summary`, `## Problem Statement`,
   the scope boundary of what the RFE covers).
2. **A technology may appear inside an acceptance criterion only as illustration** —
   wrapped in `(e.g., …)` with at least one alternative listed — **or** as the
   pre-existing platform component the criterion operates against.
3. **A technology may NEVER be the subject or the object of an acceptance criterion.**
   Every criterion states an outcome the user can observe; the reviewer must be unable
   to tell which product you would build it with.
4. **`### In Scope` lists capabilities, never mechanisms.** Delete any line naming a
   base class, an abstraction or registry, a design pattern, a framework, a transport,
   a method signature, an attribute or field name, a version pin, or a latency/
   throughput number. Those belong in the engineering design, not the RFE.

Worked example — a request that arrived naming one tracking product throughout:

WRONG — scores Open-to-HOW 1/2. The product is the object of every criterion, and
In Scope names mechanisms:

```markdown
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Training runs are logged to MLflow automatically
- [ ] Users can view training metrics in the MLflow UI
- [ ] Artifacts are browsable through MLflow's Artifacts interface

### In Scope
- TrackingBackend abstraction and registry for pluggable backends
- Cluster-level configuration via the SDK `create_cluster()` call
- Metrics streamed over Server-Sent Events with TTFT < 200ms
```

RIGHT — scores Open-to-HOW 2/2. Same need, same vocabulary, no mandated solution:

```markdown
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Data scientists can compare parameters and metrics across training runs from
      the platform UI, with no code changes to an existing training script
- [ ] Data scientists can browse and download the artifacts a run produced
- [ ] Platform administrators can choose the tracking backend a project uses
      (e.g., MLflow, Weights & Biases, TensorBoard)

### In Scope
- Automatic capture of parameters, metrics and artifacts for training runs
- Per-project selection of a tracking backend
- Cross-run comparison and filtering for the teams that own the runs
```

Note what survived: the product is still named, as one option among several, and the
criteria still describe exactly the same user outcomes. Nothing about the business need
was softened — only the choice of implementation was handed back to engineering.

## Size Guide

- **S** (Small): A focused, well-understood need. 1-2 acceptance criteria. Use the Concise format.
- **M** (Medium): A clear need with some nuance. 3-5 acceptance criteria. Use the Standard format.
- **L** (Large): A significant need spanning multiple user scenarios. 5-8 acceptance criteria. Use the Full format.
- **XL** (Extra Large): A major initiative with broad impact. 8+ acceptance criteria. Use the Full format with all optional sections.

---

## Concise Format (S)

```markdown
## Summary
<2-3 sentences: what the user needs and why>

## Affected Customers
<Named customers, segments, or partners>

## Business Justification
<Why this matters: revenue, customer commitment, strategic investment, competitive need>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>
```

---

## Standard Format (M)

```markdown
## Summary
<What the user needs and why, in enough detail to be unambiguous>

## Problem Statement
<What users cannot do today, or what is painful. Describe from the user's perspective.>

## Affected Customers
<Named customers, segments, or partners. Include scale/impact where known.>

## Business Justification
<Evidence-based: revenue impact, customer commitments, strategic investments, competitive positioning. Not assertions — data or named sources.>

## User Scenarios
<1-2 concrete scenarios: As a [role], I need to [action] because [reason]>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion — starts with the user as subject>
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>

## Success Criteria
<How do we know the problem is solved? Measurable outcomes.>

## Scope
### In Scope
<What this RFE covers>

### Out of Scope
<What this RFE explicitly does NOT cover>
```

---

## Full Format (L/XL)

```markdown
## Summary
<Comprehensive description of the business need>

## Problem Statement
<What users cannot do today, or what is painful. Include current workarounds if any.>

## Affected Customers
<Named customers, segments, or partners. Include:>
- Scale of impact (number of customers, revenue at risk)
- Specific customer requests or commitments if applicable

## Business Justification
<Evidence-based justification:>
- Revenue impact or opportunity
- Customer commitments or escalations
- Strategic investment alignment
- Competitive positioning
- Market data or analyst input

## User Scenarios
<Describe 2-3 concrete scenarios from the user's perspective:>
1. <Scenario: As a [role], I need to [action] because [reason]>
2. <Scenario>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>
- [ ] <User-perspective criterion>

## Success Criteria
<Measurable outcomes that indicate the problem is solved>

## Scope
### In Scope
<What this RFE covers>

### Out of Scope
<What this RFE explicitly does NOT cover — to prevent scope creep>

## Open Questions
<Questions that need answers before this can proceed>
```
